anomalies.fix: std.fs.cwd() -> std.Io.Dir.cwd() and GeneralPurposeAllocator -> std.heap.DebugAllocator are renames. std.process.argsAlloc is NOT: it becomes std.process.Args with toSlice(arena)/iterate(), an Io-shaped redesign. So the migration is not mechanical and cannot be scripted wholesale.
anomalies.caution: 151 files is the grep count, not the compile count — a file may use the call inside dead code or behind comptime. Size it by compiling, not by grepping. See memory pattern-defines-its-own-scope.
anomalies.method_correction: `zig test` on a file with NO test blocks analyses nothing -- main() is never compiled, so it reports success on code that cannot build. My first baseline was vacuous because of this. Use `zig build-exe <f> -femit-bin=/dev/null`. And each error masks the next: cell_trends.zig showed one trivial var/const error, and only after fixing it did the real argsAlloc breakage appear -- the fs.cwd() call on line 39 is still masked behind that.
anomalies.real_shape: NOT a rename job. Zig 0.16 introduced explicit Io passing: `Args` arrives as a parameter of main (`pub fn main(init: std.process.Minimal) !void`), and I/O entry points take an `Io` value (e.g. `std.process.currentPath(io, buffer)`). So every main() changes signature and `io` must be threaded to anything doing file or process I/O. File-by-file mechanical migration is not possible; this is an architectural decision about how the CLI carries Io.
anomalies.revised_estimate: Structural. The '751 call sites' figure describes touch points, not effort, and understates the coupling.
anomalies.resolved_pattern_2026-09-04: PROVEN WORKING (first confirmed instance in this repo, verified by compiling and running, not just reading docs): `pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !u8 { const argv = try init.minimal.args.toSlice(init.arena.allocator()); const bytes = try std.Io.Dir.cwd().readFileAlloc(init.io, path, init.gpa, .limited(n)); ... }`. init.io is a ready-to-use Io (std.Io.Threaded set up by start.zig automatically -- no manual Threaded.init/deinit needed). Used successfully in src/tri/tri_loopstate_main.zig (compiles, runs, reads real files). This resolves the PATTERN uncertainty for new standalone tools, not the scope: main.zig itself (1767 lines, old argsAlloc-based) and its ~650 siblings are unmigrated and this does not attempt that. patch_AP_kept_a_silent_infinite_loop_bug.what: Found by accident while verifying the @pow fix's artifact, not by any error message -- this class produces NO compiler error at all. `var i : usize = BASE_FEATURE_COUNT; while (i < EMBEDDING_DIM) : (i += 1) { ...i... }` in memory/formula_embed.t27 was emitted as `while (BASE_FEATURE_COUNT < EMBEDDING_DIM) : (i += 1) { ...BASE_FEATURE_COUNT... }` -- EVERY read of `i`, including the loop's OWN CONDITION, replaced by `BASE_FEATURE_COUNT`. Since `BASE_FEATURE_COUNT` never changes, the condition is constant: an infinite loop if true (the ordinary case -- EMBEDDING_DIM padding out from a smaller base count), dead code if false. Inside the body, `i - BASE_FEATURE_COUNT + 1` became `BASE_FEATURE_COUNT - BASE_FEATURE_COUNT + 1`, always exactly 1.
patch_AP_kept_a_silent_infinite_loop_bug.root_cause: `copy_propagate`'s `collect_written` set is built from `assign_root`, which only recognises `NodeKind::StmtAssign` -- a while loop's CONTINUE EXPRESSION (`: (i += 1)`) is stored as raw TEXT in `extra_op` (patch Q, this project's convention), invisible to that walk. `var i = BASE_FEATURE_COUNT;` then looked like `i` was never written anywhere in the block, satisfying copy_propagate's safety check, and every subsequent read of `i` got substituted with `BASE_FEATURE_COUNT`. This is the EXACT SAME blind spot already fixed on the READ side for `dead_store_elim` (patch Z, earlier session): a continue expression's effect is invisible to any AST walk that only inspects `.children`.
patch_AP_kept_a_silent_infinite_loop_bug.fix: Reused `while_continue_assigns` -- ALREADY proven correct for this blind spot on the read side -- verbatim, as an additional guard on copy_propagate's replacement candidates: `!stmts.iter().any(|s| while_continue_assigns(s, &stmt.name))`. No new text-scanning logic invented; the existing, tested helper answers exactly the question needed here too.
